client: I've been really struggling since I failed that exam last semester — it's like this constant knot in my stomach that won't go away. I keep thinking about what happens if I lose my scholarship, and my mind just spirals into all these worst-case scenarios. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I had to try something.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds genuinely heavy — that constant knot, the spiraling thoughts about your scholarship, and even the uncertainty about whether talking will help at all takes real courage to show up with. It makes a lot of sense that your mind keeps pulling toward worst-case scenarios when something that matters so much to you feels threatened. I'm glad you decided to try, and I'd love to start by gently exploring those spiraling thoughts together — what tends to be the very first thought that kicks off the spiral for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess the first thought is usually something like "what if I fail the next exam and my GPA drops below the cutoff." It kind of comes out of nowhere, even when I'm not doing anything school-related, like I'll just be trying to watch TV or eat dinner and suddenly it's there. And then it just snowballs from that one thought into this whole picture of losing the scholarship, having to tell my parents, maybe having to drop out entirely.
therapist: That "out of nowhere" quality is one of the most exhausting parts — your mind won't even give you a break during the small, ordinary moments that are supposed to feel safe. What you're describing sounds like a classic thought spiral, where one "what if" becomes a whole story about the worst possible ending before you've even had a chance to catch your breath. I'm curious — when that first thought shows up uninvited, what do you usually do with it, do you tend to try to push it away, or does part of you feel almost pulled to follow it all the way down?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, I think I do both, which is probably why it's so exhausting. I try to push it away at first, like I tell myself "stop, this is stupid, don't go there," but that almost never works and then I end up following it all the way down anyway, like I can't help it. It's like the harder I try to shut it out, the louder it gets, and then I'm ten steps deep into imagining some terrible outcome before I even realize what happened.
therapist: What you're describing — that push-pull exhaustion — actually makes complete sense, because trying to forcefully suppress a thought often gives it more power, not less, which is something we can definitely work with together. It sounds like part of you is also being pretty hard on yourself when the thought shows up, calling it "stupid," and I wonder if that self-criticism adds another layer of weight on top of the anxiety itself. What do you think it would feel like to respond to that first thought with a little more curiosity instead of trying to shut it down — does that feel possible, or does it feel like that would just let it win?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, when you say "respond with curiosity," my first reaction is that it sounds a little too... soft, I guess? Like if I just get curious about the thought, it feels like I'm giving it permission to stick around and grow, which is exactly what I don't want. But I can also kind of see what you mean about the self-criticism making it worse, because after I call myself stupid for having the thought, I usually end up feeling guilty on top of anxious, and then it's like a whole spiral.
therapist: That pushback makes a lot of sense, and I want to honor it — curiosity isn't about rolling out a welcome mat for the thought, it's more like observing it from a slight distance rather than either fighting it or following it down the rabbit hole. And you've already spotted something really important on your own: that the self-criticism doesn't stop the spiral, it actually fuels it by adding guilt to the anxiety, which is a genuinely useful thing to notice. So I'm wondering — if calling yourself "stupid" for having the thought isn't working, what do you think it would look like to just... acknowledge the thought showed up, without the judgment attached?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me gets it logically — like, okay, just notice the thought, don't pile on. But honestly, when I'm in the middle of it, that distance you're describing feels almost impossible to find, like I'm already ten steps into the spiral before I even realize it's happening. And I guess I'm not sure what "acknowledging without judgment" actually looks like in practice — it sounds nice here, but in the moment it feels like it would just be... letting the anxiety win?
therapist: The way you're describing it — already ten steps in before you even notice — tells me the spiral moves really fast for you, and that's actually really important information, because it means the goal isn't to catch the thought at step one every time, but to gradually build in a tiny pause earlier and earlier. "Acknowledging without judgment" in practice might look as simple as saying to yourself "there's that thought again" — not welcoming it, not fighting it, just naming it like you'd name a weather pattern outside your window. Would you be open to trying that just once this week, not to fix the spiral, but just to see if you can spot the thought and name it, even if it's already at step three or four?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I mean, I guess I can try that, but honestly, by the time I notice the spiral at all, I'm usually already in full panic mode about whether I said something wrong to someone or if they're secretly mad at me. It feels kind of pointless to just name it when the feeling is already so loud and overwhelming. Like, saying "there's that thought again" seems almost too small to matter when everything inside me is screaming that I've ruined a friendship or something.
therapist: It's really meaningful that you're willing to try, even when it feels pointless — and I notice you've just introduced something new here, this fear about friendships and whether you've upset someone, which sounds like it carries its own particular kind of pain alongside the school stuff. You're right that "naming it" feels tiny against something that loud, but I'd gently offer that the goal isn't to silence the feeling — it's just to create one small crack of space between you and it, even briefly. I'm curious, when that fear about a friendship shows up — that someone might be secretly mad at you — what does the evidence usually look like when you look back on it later, does it tend to match how certain the panic felt in the moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, when I look back on it later, most of the time there was nothing actually wrong — they weren't mad at me at all, and I'd just been spiraling for days over nothing. But in the moment it feels so real and so certain, like I just *know* something is off, even when I can't point to anything concrete. I guess that's kind of embarrassing to admit, because it makes me sound like I can't trust my own mind.
therapist: What you just noticed — that the certainty in the moment almost never matches reality afterward — is actually one of the most important insights in this whole process, and it took real honesty to say it out loud. I want to gently push back on the "embarrassing" part though, because what you're describing isn't a broken mind, it's a mind that's working overtime to protect you from threat, even when the threat isn't really there. What if, instead of "I can't trust my mind," the story was something more like "my mind sometimes sends false alarms, and I'm learning to tell the difference"?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and honestly, "false alarms" is a less harsh way to put it than what I usually tell myself. But I guess my worry is... if I start thinking of it that way, will I just let my guard down and miss something that's actually real? Like, what if one of those times the anxiety is actually right, and I've talked myself out of taking it seriously?
therapist: That's such a natural and understandable fear, and it actually speaks to how much you care about staying connected and aware — you don't want to miss something that matters. Here's what's worth considering though: your anxiety isn't currently helping you catch the real moments, because it's crying wolf so often that everything feels equally urgent and certain, which actually makes it *harder* to notice when something genuinely needs attention. What if learning to question the false alarms isn't letting your guard down, but actually sharpening your ability to tell the difference?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's true, but I'm not sure I trust myself to know the difference between a real alarm and a false one. Like, what if I start dismissing things and I miss something actually important about my health? That's exactly what scares me — that the moment I let my guard down is the moment something real slips through.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — there's a real urgency in it, like this fear about missing something important with your health feels very alive and close, not just theoretical. I want to gently notice that the worry has shifted from exams, to friendships, and now to your health, and I'm wondering if that pattern itself might be telling us something important — not that any of these fears are wrong, but that your mind may be very practiced at finding the next thing to stand guard over. Does that resonate at all, that sense of the anxiety always finding a new door to stand in front of?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean... yeah, when you put it that way, I can kind of see what you're describing. It's like as soon as I manage to push one worry down, something else just slides right into its place, and I don't even notice it happening until I'm already deep in it. But I guess part of me wonders — what if it's not just anxiety, what if some of these things actually do need watching? Like, how do I tell the difference between legitimate concern and my mind just doing its thing?
therapist: You've just described something really significant — that the anxiety is like a shape-shifter, always finding a new host, and recognizing that pattern *is* actually the beginning of being able to tell the difference. A legitimate concern tends to have some concrete evidence attached to it and usually responds to reassurance or action, whereas anxiety's version tends to feel urgent and certain but stays just as loud even after you've checked. I'm curious — when you imagine actually sitting with that question of "is this real or is this my mind doing its thing," what comes up for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
